Based on my research, **Tokyo** is the world's most populous national capital city (with approximately 14+ million residents in the city proper, and over 37 million in the metropolitan area).

Regarding when Tokyo was established:

According to the Wikipedia encyclopedia entry on Tokyo, the city was officially established in **1457**. This marks when Ōta Dōkan (a samurai, military tactician, and Buddhist monk) built Edo Castle, which is considered the origin of the city. 

Here are the key historical milestones:

| Year | Event |
|------|-------|
| Late 12th century | The village of Edo was first established by the Edo clan |
| **1457** | Ōta Dōkan built Edo Castle; the city's formal foundation |
| 1603 | Tokugawa Ieyasu established the shogunate in Edo, making it Japan's de facto political center |
| 1868 | After the Meiji Restoration, Edo was renamed Tokyo ("Eastern Capital") and became Japan's official imperial capital |

So while the area had been inhabited earlier, **1457** is recognized as the official establishment year of Tokyo/Edo as an organized city with its castle complex that would grow into the world's largest capital.

The list of world capitals includes many counties, territories, and semi-autonomous places around the globe. The list of world capitals exceeds the official number of recognized countries due to territories being included on the list. The largest capital city in the world is Beijing, China and the most remote capital is Adamstown, in the island nation of Pitcairn. Some countries, like Turkey, can be in more than one continent. The easiest way to learn the list of world capitals is to divide them into continents. The continent division is: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania. ## Trends in Urban Living
Cities are the center of human life. In 2020, 56% of the world's population lived in urban areas, and this percentage is much higher in western countries. In the United States, for example, 83% of the population lives in urban areas.

## Largest Capital Cities
The five largest capital cities in the world are Beijing, Tokyo, Moscow, Seoul, and Jakarta. The largest western capital city is London.
**Beijing** is the capital of China, and has an estimated population of 21 million people as of 2022. This makes it the fifth largest city on the globe, and the largest capital. It's one of the oldest cities in the world, having been established at least 3,000 years ago. Controlled directly by the national government, it's considered to be the nation's political, educational, and cultural center. It has been the heart of China for eight centuries, longer than almost every capital in the world. A significant problem facing Beijing today is its poor air quality due to coal burning. Smog warnings are common.
**Tokyo** is the capital of Japan, and has a population of about 14 million people in the city proper as of 2022. It is the largest city in Japan and is home to both the Japanese government and the emperor. It is a hub for the world's economy, boasting 51 Fortune 500 companies. It's also one of the more pleasant cities to visit and is rated highly in terms of friendliness, cleanliness, public transportation, nightlife, and shopping. But as a result, it's also one of the most expensive cities to live in worldwide.
**Moscow** is the capital of Russia and has a population of over 12 million people according to a 2022 estimate. It's the largest city in Europe and is a major political, cultural, and economic center. It has particularly interesting architecture since it has both modern skyscrapers, including the tallest freestanding structure in Europe, and historic buildings like the Kremlin, St. Basil's Cathedral, and Red Square. The city is almost 900 years old.
**Jakarta** is the capital of Indonesia and has a population of around 11 million people as of 2022. It's a supremely old city, existing at least since the fourth century. Today it's one of the most rapidly growing cities in the world. Unlike most of the other cities, relatively few international tourists visit Jakarta.

## Largest Capital Cities
**Seoul** is the capital of South Korea, and has a population of 10 million people as of 2022. It's home to a full five UNESCO World Heritage sites, including Changdeok Palace and Hwaseong Fortress. It's also one of the most visited cities in the world and an important center of modern culture and technology. It hosts more art openings per square mile than any city and is considered to be the seventh most sustainable city in the world.

## Largest Capital Cities
The five largest capital cities in the world are Beijing, Tokyo, Moscow, Seoul, and Jakarta. The largest western capital city is London.
**Beijing** is the capital of China, and has an estimated population of 21 million people as of 2022. This makes it the fifth largest city on the globe, and the largest capital. It's one of the oldest cities in the world, having been established at least 3,000 years ago. Controlled directly by the national government, it's considered to be the nation's political, educational, and cultural center. It has been the heart of China for eight centuries, longer than almost every capital in the world. A significant problem facing Beijing today is its poor air quality due to coal burning. Smog warnings are common.
**Tokyo** is the capital of Japan, and has a population of about 14 million people in the city proper as of 2022. It is the largest city in Japan and is home to both the Japanese government and the emperor. It is a hub for the world's economy, boasting 51 Fortune 500 companies. It's also one of the more pleasant cities to visit and is rated highly in terms of friendliness, cleanliness, public transportation, nightlife, and shopping. But as a result, it's also one of the most expensive cities to live in worldwide.
**Moscow** is the capital of Russia and has a population of over 12 million people according to a 2022 estimate. It's the largest city in Europe and is a major political, cultural, and economic center. It has particularly interesting architecture since it has both modern skyscrapers, including the tallest freestanding structure in Europe, and historic buildings like the Kremlin, St. Basil's Cathedral, and Red Square. The city is almost 900 years old.
**Jakarta** is the capital of Indonesia and has a population of around 11 million people as of 2022. It's a supremely old city, existing at least since the fourth century. Today it's one of the most rapidly growing cities in the world. Unlike most of the other cities, relatively few international tourists visit Jakarta.
texts.30:
## Largest Capital Cities
**Seoul** is the capital of South Korea, and has a population of 10 million people as of 2022. It's home to a full five UNESCO World Heritage sites, including Changdeok Palace and Hwaseong Fortress. It's also one of the most visited cities in the world and an important center of modern culture and technology. It hosts more art openings per square mile than any city and is considered to be the seventh most sustainable city in the world.

## Largest Capital Cities
The five largest capital cities in the world are Beijing, Tokyo, Moscow, Seoul, and Jakarta. The largest western capital city is London.
**Beijing** is the capital of China, and has an estimated population of 21 million people as of 2022. This makes it the fifth largest city on the globe, and the largest capital. It's one of the oldest cities in the world, having been established at least 3,000 years ago. Controlled directly by the national government, it's considered to be the nation's political, educational, and cultural center. It has been the heart of China for eight centuries, longer than almost every capital in the world. A significant problem facing Beijing today is its poor air quality due to coal burning. Smog warnings are common.
**Tokyo** is the capital of Japan, and has a population of about 14 million people in the city proper as of 2022. It is the largest city in Japan and is home to both the Japanese government and the emperor. It is a hub for the world's economy, boasting 51 Fortune 500 companies. It's also one of the more pleasant cities to visit and is rated highly in terms of friendliness, cleanliness, public transportation, nightlife, and shopping. But as a result, it's also one of the most expensive cities to live in worldwide.
**Moscow** is the capital of Russia and has a population of over 12 million people according to a 2022 estimate. It's the largest city in Europe and is a major political, cultural, and economic center. It has particularly interesting architecture since it has both modern skyscrapers, including the tallest freestanding structure in Europe, and historic buildings like the Kremlin, St. Basil's Cathedral, and Red Square. The city is almost 900 years old.
**Jakarta** is the capital of Indonesia and has a population of around 11 million people as of 2022. It's a supremely old city, existing at least since the fourth century. Today it's one of the most rapidly growing cities in the world. Unlike most of the other cities, relatively few international tourists visit Jakarta.

## Largest Capital Cities
**Seoul** is the capital of South Korea, and has a population of 10 million people as of 2022. It's home to a full five UNESCO World Heritage sites, including Changdeok Palace and Hwaseong Fortress. It's also one of the most visited cities in the world and an important center of modern culture and technology. It hosts more art openings per square mile than any city and is considered to be the seventh most sustainable city in the world.

Tokyo is one of the largest cities in the world with a population of about 14 million people. Tokyo was once called Edo, and in the late 12th century, the Edo clan created the village of Edo (the Edo clan took its name from the area called Edo.). The following is a summary of the history of Tokyo, from a small fishing village to the dramatic changes it underwent to become the Tokyo of today.
You can also learn about the history of Tokyo by watching the video below.

## Edo Castle and Edo Era
In the latter half of the 12th century, the Edo clan established the village Edo. And after a while, Edo Castle (part of the current Tokyo Imperial Palace) was built by Ota Dokan in 1457, and later became a branch castle of the Hojo clan in 1524, and the Hojo clan was destroyed in 1590 when Hideyoshi Toyotomi conquered Odawara. In 1590, Hideyoshi Toyotomi defeated the Hojo clan in Odawara, and Ieyasu Tokugawa moved the castle to his former domain, the so-called Kanpachi-shu, and made it his residence. In this way, the history of Edo changed dramatically.
When Ieyasu made the castle as his residence, the castle was only temporarily repaired however, it was later expanded and improved during the reigns of Hidetada (the 2nd) and Iemitsu (the 3rd) , and the large castle was completed in 1636 during the reign of Iemitsu. Edo era started in 1603 and lasted until 1868. If you would like to learn about sustainability in Edo era, please check "Sustainable Lifestyles in Edo and Japanese History".

## Edo Castle and Edo Era
### Ieyasu Tokugawa and Edo
By this time, Edo, the city Ieyasu had chosen as his home, was even more desolate than it had been since Dokan Ota had built his castle, and the sea was so close to the edge of the castle that it was difficult to secure fresh water, the most essential human resource.
However, Ieyasu came up with a plan. There were several small mountains in Tokyo at that time. He thought it would be easier to expand the land if he could use one of the largest mountains, called Kanda Mountain, to reclaim the sea. By cutting down the mountain and reclaiming the land to the sea, the once bumpy city of Edo was able to secure a space where residences could be built around the Edo Castle.
Furthermore, the problem of not being able to use fresh water was solved when Ieyasu drew water from Inokashira Pond through Kanda Jyosui (river). When Ieyasu opened the shogunate in Edo in 1603, the city's prosperity was assured, and by 1609 it was already a major city with 150,000 inhabitants. What was once a small fishing village had grown to house one million people by 1721.
Edo became the center of Japan, and for over 200 years, Edo enjoyed a period of peace known as the "Tokugawa Era".

## Edo Castle and Edo Era
### Edo Culture
Before the Edo era, the center of culture was Kyoto, Osaka, and other parts of the Kamigata region, but as the Edo period approached its latter stages, a culture centered in Edo began to flourish. For example, the most famous example would be kabuki. Kabuki was first performed in Kyoto in 1603, then started in Edo in 1624.
In the Edo era, Ukiyoe prints became popular as well, especially Toshusai Sharaku, Utagawa Hiroshige, and Katsushika Hokusai are particularly famous. Sumo, Rakugo also became popular in Edo era. There are many cultures blossomed in the Edo era, creating a state befitting the center of Japan.

The above photo is Chiyoda Inari Shrine. When Dokan Ota built Edo Castle in 1457, Fushimi Inari from Kyoto was transferred into the castle. Later, in 1602, when Ieyasu Tokugawa expanded Edo Castle, the shrine moved from the castle to Shibuya Miyamasu-cho.

## Edo Castle and Edo Era
### Japan was not entirely closed to other countries
It is said that Japan was closed to other countries during this period, but it did not close the country completely. It adopted a policy of trade restriction and traded with the Netherlands, China and Korea. Despite its limited diplomacy, Japan received a significant amount of foreign information.

## Opening Ports

In 1853, an American warship led by Matthew C. Perry appeared off the coast of Uraga, the entrance to Edo Bay. Perry presented the president's letter of intent to the shogunate and pressed for the opening of the country.
The following year, in 1854, Perry showed up again, and Japan signed the Treaty of Amity between the United States and Japan, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate. The U.S. demanded that the U.S.-Japan Treaty of Amity and Commerce (1858) be signed in order to further promote trade, and in addition to the two ports, five other ports (Yokohama, Nagasaki, Niigata, and Kobe) were opened to free trade.
The shogunate also signed the same treaty with the Netherlands, Russia, England, and France.

## The End of Edo Era
Takamori Saigo of the Satsuma Clan and Kogoro Katsura of the Choshu Clan joined forces to form the Satcho Alliance. With the two powerful clans united, the movement to "overthrow the Shogunate" accelerated.
In 1867, the shogun, Yoshinobu Tokugawa, returned power to the imperial court. The shogun is the "Seii Taishogun," a position given to him by the Imperial Court, and with the return of this position, the power to conduct politics was transferred to the Imperial Court.
With the return of power to the imperial court by Yoshinobu Tokugawa, it marked the end of the samurai government that had lasted for about 700 years since the Kamakura period.

## Tokyo as New Capital
After the departure of Yoshinobu Tokugawa, the new government forces moved into Edo, and an administrative district called Edo Prefecture was established.
At this time, the idea of relocating the capital from Kyoto to a more suitable area for the creation of a new Japan was also raised, and a location for the relocation of the capital was sought. In the midst of this situation, a proposal to divide the capital functions between Edo and Kyoto, and rename Kyoto as Nishikyo and Edo as Tokyo was submitted.
The proposal was approved, and the capital was moved to Edo on July 17, 1868. The name was also changed from Edo to Tokyo, and the history of Tokyo began.

## Meiji Era
This is how Tokyo began its history as the capital of Japan, but as the Meiji era began, Western culture was put to full practical use, and the infrastructure was improved with the opening of the railroad between Shimbashi and Yokohama in 1872, and the number of modern brick buildings increased rapidly.

In 1878, the city of Tokyo was established with a focus on the areas of Tokyo Prefecture that had developed as urban areas, and 15 new wards were created, eventually forming the 23 wards of today's Tokyo.
_Nihonbashi Main Street from 1911 東京風景（国立国会図書館）_

## The Great Kanto Earthquake and the War
Tokyo became the capital of Japan in this way, but in the Taisho and early Showa eras, the city was often severely damaged by wartime disasters and earthquakes, but each time it recovered and eventually grew to become the world's largest city. By the 1920s, Tokyo's population had surpassed 3.7 million.
On September 1, 1923, a massive earthquake struck Tokyo and the rest of the Kanto region. The so-called Great Kanto Earthquake occurred, leaving more than 100,000 people dead or missing, and fires broke out, turning the city into a sea of fire and devastating it. However, Shinpei Goto, who was the mayor of Tokyo at the time, planned a new city and successfully rebuilt it.

In 1941, the Pacific War broke out, and incendiary bombs began raining down on Tokyo, burned the city of densely built wooden houses to the ground. On March 10, 1945, the city of Tokyo was completely destroyed in an air raid. Tokyo was devastated and 100,000 people died. After the War, the rebuilding of the city began to center on Tokyo, and by 1955, the city of Tokyo was back on its feet.

## Post-War Reconstruction to Modern Age
As Japan entered a period of high economic growth, the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the opening of the Shinkansen bullet train, the construction of expressways, and the expansion of Tokyo's urban areas all contributed to the city's rapid development. In the latter half of the 1980s, the bubble economy caused the price of land in Tokyo to skyrocket, and the collapse of the bubble economy in 1991 caused some negative effects, such as the appearance of vacant lots everywhere.
Until the 1600s, Tokyo (Edo) was a small village. Tokyo was burned out and destroyed by the earthquakes and the War however, every time people have worked on rebuilding Tokyo and it is developing still now. The population of Tokyo has grown to around 14 million in the last 400 years.

## Is it True that Tokyo is NOT the Capital of Japan?
In 1950, it was clearly stated in the Capital Construction Law that Tokyo was the national capital however, this was abolished in 1956. In the subsequent Metropolitan Area Development Law, the wide area around Tokyo, including the Tokyo metropolitan area, is defined as the metropolitan area, but the article defining it as the capital has been lost. For this reason, we cannot clearly state that Tokyo is the capital.
Nevertheless, Tokyo is the capital in fact and form, and the official position of the Japanese government is that "Although there is no law directly stipulating that the capital is Tokyo, we believe that it is widely accepted by society as a whole that Tokyo is the capital of Japan".

Tokyo,[a] officially the Tokyo Metropolis,[b] is the capital and most populous city of Japan. The population of the city proper was over 14 million as of 2023. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.[13]
Lying at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region, on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. It is Japan's economic center and the seat of the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government administers Tokyo's central 23 special wards, which formerly made up Tokyo City; various commuter towns and suburbs in its western area; and two outlying island chains, the Tokyo Islands. Although most of the world recognizes Tokyo as a city, since 1943 its governing structure has been more akin to that of a prefecture, with an accompanying Governor and Assembly taking precedence over the smaller municipal governments that make up the metropolis. Special wards in Tokyo include Chiyoda, the site of the National Diet Building and the Tokyo Imperial Palace; Shinjuku, the city's administrative center; and Shibuya, a hub of commerce and business.

Tokyo, originally known as Edo, rose to political prominence in 1603 when it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and by the mid-18th century, Edo had evolved from a small fishing village into one of the largest cities in the world, with a population surpassing one million. After the Meiji Restoration (1868), the imperial capital in Kyoto was moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo (lit. 'Eastern Capital'). Tokyo was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing raids during World War II. Beginning in the late 1940s, Tokyo underwent rapid reconstruction and expansion, which fueled the Japanese economic miracle, in which Japan's economy became the second-largest in the world at the time, behind that of the United States.[14] As of 2025, Tokyo is home to 26 of the world's 500 largest companies, as listed in the annual Fortune Global 500.[15]
Tokyo was the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and also hosted in 2021. It hosted three G7 summits in 1979, 1986, and 1993. Tokyo is an international hub of research and development and an academic center, with several major universities, including the University of Tokyo, the top-ranking university in Japan.[16][17] Tokyo Station is the central hub for the Shinkansen, the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station. Tokyo Skytree is the world's tallest tower.[18] The Tokyo Metro Ginza Line, which opened in 1927, is the oldest underground metro line in Asia.[19]

This essay provides a brief introduction to the history of a place at 35.6762° North, 139.6503° East. Exactly, Tōkyō. The following guide offers a comprehensive explanation of the transformation the city undertook from the decline of Edo onwards. The ascent of imperial Tōkyō is briefly depicted in the mirror of the introduction of Western architecture (1), the evolution of the inner-city transport system (2) and the organization of the urban space (3). Thus, the birth of the modern world capital Tōkyō is laid out for the contemporary visitor that is keen to discover the history and evolution of the urban heritage of this modern world capital ready for staging the 2020 Olympic Games.
**Focus on Japanese Cities**
Research regarding Edo and Tōkyō is extremely extensive: For centuries, urban research in architecture, anthropology, sociology, geography, Japanese Studies and even humanities like philology and arts have produced an abundant amount of literature on this city. This interest is predominantly fueled by the extraordinary development of urban Japan. As early as in sixteenth century Japanese cities had gained a paramount importance over rural Japan — even if in the mirror of a Japanese hinterland becoming increasingly accessible to Western research recent regional studies picked up momentum. To be fair it is mainly the wealth of Japan’s economy and culture that made academics as well as the general public interested in the exploration of Japan’s urban culture. And by sheer number alone the megacity Tōkyō has become one of the most important global hubs since the beginning of the Meiji period. Especially since the economic growth in the post-war period made large part of the financial flows cross the city. Many more strategic decisions affecting people far beyond the Pacific region are made here. No wonder academics around the world have an interest in exploring the various aspects of this city:
**Overview Urban Research on Tokyo**

In German-speaking countries, this interest is shared by various researchers and institutes.[[1]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn1) First to mention are the activities of the Duisburg Institute for East Asian Studies. Back in the 1960s, Peter Schöller’s exploration of Japan’s urban spaces had inspired a whole generation of young scientists, among whom: Winfried Flüchter for urban planning and land reclamation and the research on urban planning by Uta Hohn and Carola Hein are important contributions. In French, among others, Augustin Berque offers a remarkable account of architectural theory. There is also Nicolas Fiévé’s work on urban history and Phillipe Pons on urban sociology. Among the abundant English contributions are for instance William Coaldrake on power structure, Henri Smith II on architectural theory, and for urban and architectural history David Stewart, Edward Seidensticker, Roman Cybrinsky, Kenneth Frampton, James Hoare. Jinnai Hidenobu, Dōmon Fuyuji, Hasegawa Takashi, Fujita Hiroo, Muramatsu Shin and Fujimori Terunobu are among the many Japanese city historians who pay particular attention to the history, practice, law, demography and planning culture of Japanese urban development.

## 1 Tokyo before Meiji, 1457–1868
As already mentioned above, Tōkyō before the ascent of Imperial Japan throughout the Meiji time was called Edo.[**[2]**](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn2) For centuries this castle town near the river delta of Eastern Kantō was the destination of annual processions (_sankin kōtai_). These pilgrimages occurred throughout the year from all over Japan to pay respect to the Tokugawa Shoguns and their followers. Edo was only renamed Tōkyō after the Restauration of the Imperial household with Emperor Meiji Mutsuhito as house herald in 1868. [[3]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn3) Edo’s story can be divided into the following periods:
**1.1 City Foundation, 1457–1602**
The city founding of today’s Tōkyōs goes back to Ōta Dōkan (1432–1486). This samurai was a military tactician and Buddhist monk turned poet who declared a strategically located fishing village in the center of the Kantō plain as his seat of rule. The first castle complex he built near the banks of a river called Sumidagawa is considered to be the origin of Edo. Throughout the years a modest castle town (_jōkamachi_) developed around this rudimentary castle complex. In late sixteenth century Edo was taken under the rule of the Tokugawa gaining its importance as shogunal capital and political center of Japan only after the victory of Tokugawa Ieyasu in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1603.
**1.2 Edo and the Tokugawa, 1603–1853**

## 1 Tokyo before Meiji, 1457–1868
Under the rule of the thirteen consecutive Tokugawa-Shoguns Edo knew a hitherto unprecedented population growth, even exceeding that of London and Paris at times.[[4]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn4) During the Edo period, which lasted from 1603 to 1868, various areas of the city experienced heydays and less glorious days. Except the recurring destruction to fire outbreaks, it is above all the social division of Edo that can be considered the most characteristic aspect of Edo during this epoch. The division was aimed at underlining the hierarchical structure of Tokugawa society in urban space. This resulted in divided quarters for samurai, peasants, artisans and traders (_shinōkōshō_) according to the feudal estates-based societal rules (_mibun seido_).[[5]](https://medium.com/@hamp.mathias/from-edo-to-tokyo-birth-of-a-global-capital-c9effafada34#_ftn5)
Edo organized the urban space in following parts: a castle area (1), adjacent _buke-chi_, that is districts for feudal heirs called _daimyo_(2), various temple and shrine areas _tera-machi_ or even _monzen-machi_ (3), and space for commoners (4). Tokugawa rule assigned common citizens only a narrow space at east of the castle town on the banks of Sumidagawa river and the shoreline to Edo bay (today: Tōkyō Bay). There far below the castle (_shitamachi_) a city of its own developed. Mainly for traders and craftsmen the lower city showed an incredible density. In midst of countless water channels, which drew their water partly from Sumidagawa, partly from neighboring rivers and cut through all quarters, the culture of the common people (_chōnin bunka_) with their special high places (_meisho_) developed. The urban cultural of these days consisted of entertainment districts, markets and teahouses and became the meeting place of the pleasurable Edo citizen. ## Edo Castle and Edo Era
In the latter half of the 12th century, the Edo clan established the village Edo. And after a while, Edo Castle (part of the current Tokyo Imperial Palace) was built by Ota Dokan in 1457, and later became a branch castle of the Hojo clan in 1524, and the Hojo clan was destroyed in 1590 when Hideyoshi Toyotomi conquered Odawara. In 1590, Hideyoshi Toyotomi defeated the Hojo clan in Odawara, and Ieyasu Tokugawa moved the castle to his former domain, the so-called Kanpachi-shu, and made it his residence. In this way, the history of Edo changed dramatically.
When Ieyasu made the castle as his residence, the castle was only temporarily repaired however, it was later expanded and improved during the reigns of Hidetada (the 2nd) and Iemitsu (the 3rd) , and the large castle was completed in 1636 during the reign of Iemitsu. Edo era started in 1603 and lasted until 1868. If you would like to learn about sustainability in Edo era, please check "Sustainable Lifestyles in Edo and Japanese History".
texts.2:
## Edo Castle and Edo Era
### Ieyasu Tokugawa and Edo
By this time, Edo, the city Ieyasu had chosen as his home, was even more desolate than it had been since Dokan Ota had built his castle, and the sea was so close to the edge of the castle that it was difficult to secure fresh water, the most essential human resource.
However, Ieyasu came up with a plan. There were several small mountains in Tokyo at that time. He thought it would be easier to expand the land if he could use one of the largest mountains, called Kanda Mountain, to reclaim the sea. By cutting down the mountain and reclaiming the land to the sea, the once bumpy city of Edo was able to secure a space where residences could be built around the Edo Castle.
Furthermore, the problem of not being able to use fresh water was solved when Ieyasu drew water from Inokashira Pond through Kanda Jyosui (river). When Ieyasu opened the shogunate in Edo in 1603, the city's prosperity was assured, and by 1609 it was already a major city with 150,000 inhabitants. ## Is it True that Tokyo is NOT the Capital of Japan?
In 1950, it was clearly stated in the Capital Construction Law that Tokyo was the national capital however, this was abolished in 1956. In the subsequent Metropolitan Area Development Law, the wide area around Tokyo, including the Tokyo metropolitan area, is defined as the metropolitan area, but the article defining it as the capital has been lost. For this reason, we cannot clearly state that Tokyo is the capital.
Nevertheless, Tokyo is the capital in fact and form, and the official position of the Japanese government is that "Although there is no law directly stipulating that the capital is Tokyo, we believe that it is widely accepted by society as a whole that Tokyo is the capital of Japan".

Tokyo,[a] officially the Tokyo Metropolis,[b] is the capital and most populous city of Japan. The population of the city proper was over 14 million as of 2023. The Greater Tokyo Area, which includes Tokyo and parts of six neighboring prefectures, is the third-most populous metropolitan area in the world, with 33 million residents as of 2025.[13]
Lying at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region, on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. It is Japan's economic center and the seat of the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government administers Tokyo's central 23 special wards, which formerly made up Tokyo City; various commuter towns and suburbs in its western area; and two outlying island chains, the Tokyo Islands. Although most of the world recognizes Tokyo as a city, since 1943 its governing structure has been more akin to that of a prefecture, with an accompanying Governor and Assembly taking precedence over the smaller municipal governments that make up the metropolis. Special wards in Tokyo include Chiyoda, the site of the National Diet Building and the Tokyo Imperial Palace; Shinjuku, the city's administrative center; and Shibuya, a hub of commerce and business.

Tokyo, originally known as Edo, rose to political prominence in 1603 when it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate, and by the mid-18th century, Edo had evolved from a small fishing village into one of the largest cities in the world, with a population surpassing one million. After the Meiji Restoration (1868), the imperial capital in Kyoto was moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo (lit. 'Eastern Capital'). Tokyo was greatly damaged by the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and by Allied bombing raids during World War II. Beginning in the late 1940s, Tokyo underwent rapid reconstruction and expansion, which fueled the Japanese economic miracle, in which Japan's economy became the second-largest in the world at the time, behind that of the United States.[14] As of 2025, Tokyo is home to 26 of the world's 500 largest companies, as listed in the annual Fortune Global 500.[15]
Tokyo was the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics, in 1964, and also hosted in 2021. It hosted three G7 summits in 1979, 1986, and 1993. Tokyo is an international hub of research and development and an academic center, with several major universities, including the University of Tokyo, the top-ranking university in Japan.[16][17] Tokyo Station is the central hub for the Shinkansen, the country's high-speed railway network, and the city's Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest train station.
